meta.ogDescription: Verified: Dale Carnegie wrote it in How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), Part Two, Chapter 1 — and he says it twice on the same page.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is genuine, and word-for-word. It is on page 76 of How to Win Friends and Influence People, Part Two (“Six Ways to Make People Like You”), Chapter 1 — and Carnegie says it twice in a row, the second time in exactly the wording that circulates today (1943 Bombay printing, Internet Archive ↗).

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: How to Win Friends and Influence People
Part Two (“Six Ways to Make People Like You”), Ch. 1 — p. 76 in the 1943 Bombay printing

source.excerpt: You never read a book on psychology, Tippy. You didn’t need to. You knew by some divine instinct that one can make more friends in two months by becoming genuinely interested in other people than one can in two years by trying to get other people interested in him. Let me repeat that. You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.
trail: The sentence is printed on p. 76 of the eleventh Indian edition (Bombay: D. B. Taraporevala Sons & Co., 1943), in Part Two, Chapter 1, “Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere” — full scan at the Internet Archive ↗. That printing predates the 1981 revised edition.
Wikipedia ↗ dates first publication to October 1936 by Simon & Schuster and gives the chapter’s principle as “Become genuinely interested in other people.”
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced section for the book, in a shortened form cited to p. 52 of a 1998 edition.
Quote Investigator’s Dale Carnegie file ↗ lists no entry for this line — there is no competing claim to trace.
source.excerptNote: Carnegie is addressing Tippy, the puppy of his childhood, a few lines after describing the dog’s death. The Internet Archive copy is machine-read from a 1943 scan and garbles a few characters in the second sentence; the wording given here is the standard reading, and the first sentence — with “genuinely” — is legible as printed.

author.name: Dale Carnegie
author.heading: About Dale Carnegie
author.bio: Dale Carnegie was born in Maryville, Missouri in 1888 and talked a YMCA manager into letting him teach a public-speaking class for a cut of the takings — the seed of the Dale Carnegie Course. His 1936 book How to Win Friends and Influence People turned that classroom material into one of the best-selling self-improvement books ever written; by his death in 1955 it had sold some five million copies in 31 languages. He wrote plainly and repeated himself on purpose, which is exactly why so many of his sentences survive as free-floating quotations.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right — the wording drifts
misattribution.intro: For once, a famous name actually said it. What travels instead is the wording: Carnegie wrote the sentence twice on one page, and quotation collections have since produced further condensations of both.

items.why: A compressed form — “You can make more friends in two months by being interested in them, than in two years by making them interested in you” — is what appears in the sourced section of his Wikiquote page ↗, cited there to p. 52 of a 1998 edition. It is markedly tighter than the sentence printed in the book.

Some quotations insert “genuinely” — “by becoming genuinely interested in other people.” That matches Carnegie’s first, third-person pass at the sentence on the same page, and it is the wording of the chapter’s stated principle, “Become genuinely interested in other people” (Wikipedia ↗). The popular sentence is his second pass, which drops the adverb.

misattribution.truthLine: Both are Carnegie’s, and the familiar wording is the one he printed verbatim — readable on p. 76 of the 1943 Bombay printing at the Internet Archive ↗.

context.heading: He was talking to a dog
lead: The most-quoted sentence in Carnegie’s book is addressed to a puppy. The chapter opens by asking why you would read a book about winning friends when you could instead study “the greatest winner of friends the world has ever known” — the dog who wags his tail at you from ten feet away with no real estate to sell. Carnegie then recalls Tippy, the fifty-cent yellow-haired pup his father bought when he was five, killed by lightning within ten feet of him one night, and tells him: you never read a book on psychology, and you didn’t need to.

The line lands its point immediately afterward with a piece of period data Carnegie loved: the New York Telephone Company studied 500 telephone conversations to find the most frequently used word, and it was “I.” The principle this chapter carries is the first of the six — “Become genuinely interested in other people” (Wikipedia ↗).
detailsBody: Carnegie wrote the sentence twice on the same page, and the repetition is deliberate: the first pass is third-person and includes the word “genuinely,” the second drops it and switches to “you.” Quote collections almost always take the second version, which is why the familiar wording lacks the adverb that Carnegie made the chapter’s actual principle.
context.pull: You never read a book on psychology, Tippy. You didn’t need to.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact popular wording appears in How to Win Friends and Influence People, Part Two, Chapter 1 ("Do This and You'll Be Welcome Anywhere"), on p. 76 of the eleventh Indian edition (Bombay: D. B. Taraporevala Sons & Co., 1943); Carnegie states it twice, first with 'genuinely' in the third person and then, after 'Let me repeat that', in the familiar second-person form. The surrounding passage concerns his childhood dog Tippy and the New York Telephone Company's study of 500 telephone conversations finding 'I' the most-used word.

Wikiquote's Dale Carnegie page lists, in its sourced section for How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), the shortened form 'You can make more friends in two months by being interested in them, than in two years by making them interested in you,' cited to p. 52 in a 1998 edition.

How to Win Friends and Influence People was first published in October 1936 by Simon & Schuster; the first of the six principles in Part Two, 'Six Ways to Make People Like You', is 'Become genuinely interested in other people'; a revised edition appeared in 1981 that restructured the book from six sections to four.

Dale Carnegie was born 24 November 1888 in Maryville, Missouri and died 1 November 1955; he began teaching for the YMCA in 1912, and by his death How to Win Friends and Influence People had sold five million copies in 31 languages.
Quote Investigator's Dale Carnegie category page indexes its Carnegie investigations and contains no article about this quotation or about a 'two months' friendship line.

The wording 'You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you' circulates credited to Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends & Influence People.
